1) Mint (src/app/api/account/link-discord/route.ts:21-48): POST requires a live player (requirePlayer, src/lib/auth/helpers.ts:174-177), rejects players that already have discord_id (:31-36), then mints signLinkToken(player.id, now+600s) and stores it as __poketools_link_discord (httpOnly, sameSite lax, path '/', maxAge 600). 2) Token shape (src/lib/utils/crypto.ts:27-31): the MAC is HMAC(secret, `${playerId}.${expiresAtMs}`). verifyLinkToken (:34-42) checks exactly a 3-part split, expiry, and that MAC, and returns the bare playerId. The token therefore cannot express provider, OAuth state, or the session that minted it — TTL is the only revocation. The hunter's claim here is exact.

3) Consumption (src/auth.ts:188-225): signIn returns early for non-Discord providers (:192); otherwise it reads the cookie (:194-196), deletes it (:199), verifies it (:201), reads profile.id (:207-210), and links if the Discord id has no other owner (:213-219). It never calls auth()/requirePlayer, never compares the browser's current session to playerId, and never requires the initiating session to still exist. I read lines 158-337 in full: there is no `events` key at all, so no signOut handler clears the cookie. Grep for LINK_DISCORD_COOKIE across the repo returns only src/auth.ts:23,195,199, the route (src/app/api/account/link-discord/route.ts:3,42) and route.test.ts — no revocation counterpart, and src/ contains no middleware file that could clear or gate it.

4) Result (src/auth.ts:231-258 + src/lib/supabase/queries/players.ts:87-96,133-142,160-171): linkDiscordToPlayer updates players.discord_id for playerId under `.is('discord_id', null)`; the jwt callback then calls resolveSignInPlayer({provider:'discord', id: D2}), and getSessionPlayerRowByIdentity selects the row `.eq('discord_id', D2)`, which is now P's row. So the second person's session is minted with P's playerId and P's isAdmin/isResourceAdmin/status, and because every later refresh re-reads by (discord, D2), it stays P. Guards re-read live by the same identity, so the second person exercises P's authority, not just a stale copy.

5) Controls that might have refuted it, checked: `checks: ['state']` (src/auth.ts:165) protects CSRF only and is unrelated to the link intent; the 409 at route.ts:31-36 covers only a player that already has discord_id (i.e., the initiator is a credentials player); linkDiscordToPlayer's `.is('discord_id', null)` guard prevents re-linking an already-linked row but says nothing about which human is signing in; and the existing-owner check at auth.ts:214-216 blocks only when the incoming Discord id already owns a *different* player row, which by construction is not the case for a first-time Discord user.

The precondition set is real but coincidental rather than attacker-driven: a shared/reused browser profile, an intent minted and never consumed (any cancelled or failed Discord OAuth leaves it live, since only the callback deletes it), and a second person completing Discord sign-in within 10 minutes with an account that has no player row yet. That caps likelihood, not the demonstrated impact — the impact is a full cross-principal session into the previous player's account. No unlink or change-email flow exists (docs/auth-email-password.md:74), so repair needs an admin.

Trace holds. src/app/api/players/[id]/public-profile/route.ts:13-20 does serve anonymous GETs with no auth, no rate-limit call and no publicReads lookup, and composes inline. compose.ts:52-77 issues 8 parallel reads plus two dependent chains (compose.ts:186 listTournamentsByIds, compose.ts:194-208 getParticipantsBatch + getCompletedMatchRecordsBatch + loadSeasonStandingsContexts, plus aggregates.ts:566 getGlobalKillRankForPokemon); ~14-15 round trips per request is correct. games.ts:632-641 and matches.ts:447-452 carry .limit(500). aggregates.ts:574-579 has no .limit()/.range(). next ^16.3.8 (package.json:64) and a module-level supabase client with no fetch cache (src/lib/supabase/client.ts:21-23) mean the route is genuinely uncached.

But 'unlike every comparable anonymous endpoint' is false, and that is the load-bearing premise. checkPublicRateLimit appears in exactly three places: proxy-image/route.ts:25, replay-frames/route.ts:15, calc-route.ts:44 via the /api/calc/* gate. Its own doc comment (rate-limit.ts:300-302) enumerates exactly those three, and CHANGELOG.md:134 states the limiter's scope as 'sign-in, sign-up, verification e-mails, calculators and image proxies'. The common property of the limited set is attacker-controlled outbound fetch or attacker-controlled CPU compute, not DB reads of public rows. Comparable anonymous DB-read endpoints carry no limiter either: /api/usage-stats (usage-stats/route.ts:10-38, public, unlimited, no cache header), /api/stats (stats/route.ts:28, 'Public: no auth required', edge cache at :93 but no limiter). So the route is the site-wide norm for public reads, not an outlier — the missing limiter is a design boundary, not a defeated control.

3. Cache bypass is real but not a control bypass. publicReads.playerProfile (public-reads.ts:527-546, TTL 30 s from :108) is consumed by the page ((public)/players/[id]/page.tsx:41) and, by choice, by two API routes (pokemon/[name]/stats, matches/head-to-head). No route is obliged to consume it, and nothing in the repo's client code calls /api/players/[id]/public-profile at all (whole-repo search for 'public-profile' returns only the route, its tests, the path-guard test and AGENTS.md:19) — it is a documented external public API, not a cache front door that got bypassed.

4. There is no amplification asymmetry. The only attacker-controlled input is the player UUID, which selects a key; it does not set work. Each request is bounded by data: two .limit(500) reads, one small precomputed aggregates read (scope_type='all_time' AND scope_id IS NULL — roughly one row per Pokémon, two columns, aggregates.ts:574-579; :559-565 documents it as the cheap replacement for fetching all global aggregates). 1 request = ~14 bounded queries, not N× an unbounded unit. That is the opposite of the calc/proxy/replay class where a single request can be made arbitrarily expensive.

5. The same fan-out is already served, equally uncached and unlimited, to any signed-in user via the auth twin at players/[id]/profile/route.ts:21-27, which calls the identical composePlayerProfile. The anonymous-vs-authenticated delta is one account registration, so the composition cost is a property of every profile read, not an anonymous-only exposure.

6. Impact is asserted, not established: the candidate itself says 'the source shows the disproportion but not the resulting shared-resource effect' and leaves severity null. 'How much load degrades the shared Supabase project' is a capacity measurement, not a missing control fact — resolving it cannot turn a missing-best-practice into a boundary violation. Under the skill's rules this is durability/hardening, not a finding (anti-patterns 1 and 2: checklist deviation and defense-in-depth with no reachable boundary violation), and needs_validation would be a parking place for a speculative impact claim.

No confidentiality or integrity effect is implied: the response is correctly narrowed (route.ts:29-32, toPublicProfileView) and the data served is already public. Refuted on the control premise and on missing meaningful impact, both from source.

reasoning: The mechanical write the hunter describes is real: applySuperadminOverride does persist players.is_admin=true, it runs at sign-in and on every token refresh, and no code in src/ clears the column when the env identity changes. The candidate nevertheless fails as a boundary violation on three source-established points. (1) The claimed control is false. The hunter asserts env config is 'the whole and only source' of admin authority and that durable storage 'is not needed'. The repository says the opposite: helpers.ts:24-25 documents the revocation model as 'revoking admin ... takes effect on the next guarded call' from the stored column; supabase/migrations/20261018130400_bootstrap_first_admin.sql:31-35 promotes a row to is_admin durably as the intended first-admin mechanism; and src/__tests__/auth.test.ts:332 deliberately asserts the persistence ('applies the superadmin override on refresh and persists is_admin'). The is_admin column is the primary durable role store, and the env identity is an additive per-request grant layered on it — not a lease that removal terminates. (2) The claimed missing inverse path exists. playerUpdateSchema accepts is_admin (schemas.ts:172), the PATCH handler passes the body through for any admin (route.ts:85,114 — only is_creator is superadmin-gated at 104-110) and updatePlayer writes it (players.ts:365-370). The shipped admin roster UI exposes exactly that as an admin toggle button (PlayerRoster.tsx:351-355 -> handleToggleAdmin 97-102, sending { is_admin: !player.is_admin }); the admin toggle is not behind the canManageCreators gate that guards the creator toggle (366). In the alleged scenario — env var removed — isSuperadmin() is false (helpers.ts:284-300) and applySuperadminOverride no longer runs (auth.ts:107), so that demotion sticks on the next guarded call. The operator therefore has two working revocation paths (admin PATCH/UI, direct DB), one of which is the documented one. (3) The principal is the operator's own trusted account (docs/poketools-spec.md:1473 'the operator account'), so the residual state is that account's own durable admin role, not a lower-trust principal crossing a boundary; there is no escalation beyond authority the identity already held, and no attacker-controlled input. What remains is a de-provisioning footgun (an operator who removes SUPERADMIN_DISCORD_ID expecting that to revoke, without also clearing the row), and the repo documents no such expectation. The candidate's two sub-scenarios are also mutually exclusive and conflated: silent re-promotion of a PATCH is_admin=false occurs only while the identity is still configured superadmin (where re-promotion is the intended override behaviour), and the retention scenario is exactly where demotion succeeds. Subsidiary impacts overreach: a residual is_admin cannot change is_creator, because route.ts:104-110 requires the live env-derived isSuperadmin, which it no longer satisfies. Audit-log nit, not this finding: while the env var still matches, a PATCH is_admin=false returns 200 and logAuditEvent records the demotion (route.ts:118-133) before the next refresh re-promotes silently — but that is audit inaccuracy under a still-valid configuration, not a revocation failure.

_candidate.title: Superadmin override persists is_admin on the player row, so removing SUPERADMIN_DISCORD_ID/SUPERADMIN_EMAIL never revokes site admin
_candidate.attack_class: Chained vulnerabilities and trust boundaries — revocation, rollback, and stale derived authority
_candidate.principal: A principal that was site superadmin by environment configuration (SUPERADMIN_DISCORD_ID or SUPERADMIN_EMAIL) and whose identity the operator has since removed from that configuration; the affected parties are the community/operator whose revocation is ignored (and every player row, season/tournament resource, and admin export the residual admin can still reach).
_candidate.input: One ordinary authenticated request by that identity — any sign-in or any JWT refresh (every 5 minutes of activity, or trigger 'update') while the env var still matches, which fires applySuperadminOverride and writes players.is_admin = true. After the operator removes the env var, no input is needed at all: the persisted column is the grant.
_candidate.control: The env-configured superadmin identity check (isSuperadminIdentity) is meant to be the whole and only source of that authority, and removing the identity from SUPERADMIN_DISCORD_ID / SUPERADMIN_EMAIL is the operator's only revocation lever for it. The intended control is that superadmin authority is derived at request time from configuration, not stored as durable role state; readLivePlayer (helpers.ts:74-77) already re-applies the authority in memory on every guard call, so durable storage is not needed to enforce it.
_candidate.boundary: src/auth.ts#applySuperadminOverride — the configuration-derived superadmin decision (auth.ts:93-104) is converted into a durable row-level grant (players.is_admin) with no inverse path, and that column is what the live guards trust (helpers.ts:186-192 requireAdmin).
_candidate.impact: The removed identity keeps full site-admin indefinitely: requireAdmin() passes from the live row, so it can PATCH any player including is_admin/is_creator-adjacent fields (route.ts:104-114), DELETE players and their linked Supabase Auth users (route.ts:142-214), grant/revoke resource_admins for any season or tournament (resource-admins/route.ts:50-111), and reach every admin-only read/export. Because site admins bypass the ban/suspend check (helpers.ts:94-97), banning the row is not an alternative containment either, and while the env var is still set a deliberate PATCH is_admin=false on that row is silently re-promoted within one session refresh while returning 200 and logging a 'demotion' audit entry.
_candidate.evidence: src/auth.ts:106-118 — applySuperadminOverride: when isSuperadminIdentity(identity) is true and the row is not admin, it calls updatePlayer(player.playerId, { is_admin: true }) (line 110) and also sets player.isAdmin = true (line 116); the catch at 111-114 only logs a failed write, so the session override survives it. src/auth.ts:93-104 — the superadmin decision reads process.env.SUPERADMIN_DISCORD_ID / SUPERADMIN_EMAIL at call time, which is the only grant source and the only thing an operator can change. src/auth.ts:133 and 306-309 — the override runs on initial sign-in and on every token refresh, so the column is written repeatedly. src/lib/supabase/queries/players.ts:365-384 — updatePlayer maps input.is_admin straight into the UPDATE with no privilege-side-effects handling and no compensating write. src/lib/auth/helpers.ts:70-79,186-192 — readLivePlayer adds the override in memory and requireAdmin decides from the live row's is_admin, so the stored true is fully sufficient for every guard once the env var no longer matches. src/lib/auth/helpers.ts:94-97 — isInGoodStanding returns true for any is_admin row, so a ban/suspension cannot contain the leftover admin. src/app/api/players/[id]/route.ts:104-114 and src/lib/validation/schemas.ts:167-174 — PATCH accepts is_admin and writes body verbatim for an admin, giving an apparent manual demotion that the override silently reverts while the env var stands. A repository-wide search for SUPERADMIN in src/ finds only auth.ts (plus docs and auth helpers tests); no route, cron, or migration reconciles or clears players.is_admin when the configured identity changes, which is the missing inverse path. src/__tests__/auth.test.ts:332-340 asserts the write ('persists is_admin'), confirming the persistence is real code behavior rather than a dead branch — the retention after env removal is the unconsidered consequence, not a reverted control.

reasoning: The code-level half of the trace holds exactly as described: /api/proxy-image is unauthenticated (route.ts:10), the only throttle is the 60/min per-IP public limiter (route.ts:25), the attacker-controlled url parameter (route.ts:28) is parsed and checked once against the HTTPS rule (route.ts:44-49) and the host+path-prefix allowlist (route.ts:52-60), and the fetch at route.ts:63 passes the raw `url` string with only a `signal` option. WHATWG fetch (undici under Node/Next) defaults to `redirect: "follow"` (up to 20 hops), so hops 2..n are never re-validated by this code, a 3xx to `http://` is followed, and route.ts:72-90 then treats the final response's content type and body as the proxy result. That is a genuine gap in the route's own control and it is inconsistent with the repo's sibling fetches that pin the behaviour (image-fetch.ts:97, match-card-image.tsx:71, pokepaste.ts:36). But the boundary crossing itself is not established from source. To make the proxy reach a non-allowlisted destination, an allowlisted origin must emit a 3xx whose Location the attacker chooses, and neither the path (route.ts:14-15) nor any other in-repo evidence shows that play.pokemonshowdown.com or img.pokemondb.net exposes an attacker-influenceable redirect under `/sprites/`. Neither host is repo-controlled; confirming it requires outbound probing of third-party services, which this workflow forbids. Second, the stated impact (internal-only services, cloud metadata, loopback/sidecar admin ports) depends on the deployment topology, and the repo only shows a Node build/start (package.json:11,16 `next build`/`next start`) with no deployment or network-topology definition, so reachability of any internal endpoint from the deployment host is not derivable from source. Both are specific, source-grounded blocked facts rather than a weakness in the trace, hence needs_validation with no severity. The 60/min limit and GET-only method also bound the effect materially, and a body read still requires the redirected target to answer with `image/*` (route.ts:73).

_candidate.title: Public image proxy applies its host/path allowlist only to the first URL, then follows upstream redirects to any destination
_candidate.principal: Anonymous internet visitor — `/api/proxy-image` is explicitly unauthenticated (route.ts:10 "Public: no auth required") and the only throttle is a 60-request/minute per-IP public limiter (route.ts:25).
_candidate.input: The `url` query parameter is fully attacker-controlled (route.ts:28) and is used verbatim as the fetch target (route.ts:63). The attacker supplies an allowlisted URL such as `https://play.pokemonshowdown.com/sprites/<anything>` and relies on the allowlisted origin answering with a 3xx whose `Location` the attacker influences.
_candidate.control: The intended control is the explicit destination allowlist — `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` host + `/sprites/` path-prefix pairs (route.ts:13-16), HTTPS-only (route.ts:44-49), and the host/path comparison (route.ts:52-60). The repo enforces this same class of control elsewhere by refusing redirects outright: `src/lib/social/image-fetch.ts:13` ("redirects are refused, so the allowlist cannot be bounced elsewhere") with `src/lib/social/image-fetch.ts:97` `redirect: 'error'`; `src/lib/discord/match-card-image.tsx:69-72` `redirect: 'error'`; `src/lib/ai/agent/tools/pokepaste.ts:36` `redirect: 'manual'`.
_candidate.boundary: Server → internet destination restriction in `src/app/api/proxy-image/route.ts#GET`. The check at route.ts:52-60 bounds only the pre-redirect URL; route.ts:63 passes no `redirect` option, so WHATWG/undici default `redirect: "follow"` (up to 20 hops) is in effect and the final destination is never re-validated. The HTTPS-only rule is bypassed the same way (a 302 to `http://…` is followed).
_candidate.impact: Server-side request forgery from the deployment host to any host/protocol the redirect chain selects: internal-only HTTP services, cloud metadata endpoints, or loopback/sidecar admin ports that are unreachable from the internet. Response body is returned to the attacker when the redirected target answers with an `image/*` content type (route.ts:72-78, 80-90); otherwise the distinct 502 codes (`proxy_upstream_failed` vs `proxy_upstream_not_image`) plus timing still give a reachability/status oracle for internal ports. Request volume is bounded to 60/min per client IP and state change is limited to GET. Same root cause, second reachable instance inside this unit's scope: `src/lib/avatar/transform.ts:275-282` checks `protocol`/host allowlist on the Replicate output URL, then `transform.ts:289` fetches it without pinning redirects.
_candidate.evidence: route.ts:13-16 defines `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` as host/pathPrefix pairs and the header comment states the intent "Tightly scoped: only sprite-path images from Pokémon Showdown and PokemonDB". route.ts:44-49 rejects non-`https:` initial URLs. route.ts:52-60 computes `allowed` from `parsed.hostname === o.host && parsed.pathname.startsWith(o.pathPrefix)` on the attacker-supplied URL. route.ts:63 `const response = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) })` — no `redirect` option, and `url` is the raw parameter, not the already-validated `parsed` object, so nothing re-checks the hop that actually produces the response. route.ts:72-78 reads the content type of the *final* response, and route.ts:80 buffers its body — proving the code treats post-redirect responses as normal results. By contrast `src/lib/social/image-fetch.ts:97` and `src/lib/discord/match-card-image.tsx:71` pin `redirect: 'error'`, and `image-fetch.ts:48` compares `parsed.origin` (port included) rather than `hostname`, showing the project knows both the bounce and the port-scope hazards for this exact pattern; `src/lib/avatar/transform.ts:289` is the other allowlisted fetch that omits the pin.
